column1: In sys.dm_exec_requests, a positive {{c1::blocking_session_id}} identifies an ordinary blocking session.
column2:
Use the positive ID to look up the blocking session and follow the chain. Special negative values indicate other conditions, so do not treat them as normal session IDs.
Review source

column1: The {{c1::wait_resource}} column in sys.dm_exec_requests identifies the resource a request is waiting for.
column2:
The resource identifies what the request needs, such as a locked key. The wait type describes the nature of the wait. Read them together to understand why the request cannot proceed.
Review source

column1: For a sleeping session, sys.dm_exec_sessions.open_transaction_count {{c1::greater than zero}} indicates that transactions remain open.
column2:
Sleeping means that the session is not running a request now. A nonzero count means its earlier work still holds an open transaction, which can retain locks and block other requests.
Review source

column1: To inspect the last command submitted by session 52, query {{c1::sys.dm_exec_input_buffer(52, NULL)}}.
column2:
The first argument selects session 52, and NULL omits a specific request ID. The input buffer shows submitted text, not the complete history of statements that ran in the transaction.
Review source

column1: To make qualifying runtime errors abort the transaction instead of only the failed statement, use {{c1::SET XACT_ABORT ON;}}
column2:
This setting rolls back the transaction for qualifying runtime errors instead of leaving only the failed statement undone. Compile errors are unaffected. THROW honors the setting, but RAISERROR does not.
Review source

column1: SQL Server returns error {{c1::1205}} to the transaction selected as a deadlock victim.
column2:
Error 1205 reports that SQL Server rolled back the victim transaction to break a deadlock. Retry the full transaction, not just the statement that happened to encounter the cycle.
Review source

column1: A deadlock graph's {{c1::victim-list}} identifies the process chosen as the victim.
column2:
Start with the listed process ID, then find the same ID in the process list. That connects the victim designation to the session and statement that SQL Server chose to roll back.
Review source

column1: A deadlock graph's {{c1::process-list}} contains the participating sessions' execution and transaction details.
column2:
This section identifies the participants and gives context such as their statements and transaction details. Use those IDs with the resource list to determine which locks each participant owns or waits for.
Review source

column1: In Azure SQL Database, CREATE EVENT SESSION uses the scope {{c1::ON DATABASE}}.
column2:
The database scope places the event session in the connected database rather than on the logical server. Connect to the database whose events you need before creating the session.
Review source

column1: Capture Azure SQL Database deadlock graphs with the Extended Event {{c1::sqlserver.database_xml_deadlock_report}}.
column2:
The Extended Event records an XML graph with processes and resources involved in the cycle. A database-scoped session must be running to capture new events into its configured target.
Review source

column1: For a database-scoped Extended Events session, read target data from {{c1::sys.dm_xe_database_session_targets}}.
column2:
The target view exposes data from running database-scoped sessions, such as an in-memory ring buffer. Join to the session view to select the target belonging to the intended session.
Review source

column1: In Azure SQL Database, start the existing database-scoped Extended Events session named deadlocks with {{c1::ALTER EVENT SESSION [deadlocks] ON DATABASE STATE = START;}}
column2:
CREATE EVENT SESSION defines the session. Starting it activates event collection for the current database. Setting startup behavior does not by itself start a stopped session now.
Review source

column1: After confirming that session 52 is an abandoned blocker, terminate it with {{c1::KILL 52;}}
column2:
Terminating a session can trigger rollback of its open transaction. Use this only after you confirm the session is abandoned and assess the impact of losing its uncommitted work.
Review source
